confirmed: Read the entire markdown conversion, including references and Appendices A–E, and checked the recorded numbers against PDF text. The PDF has 28 pages and identifies itself as arXiv:2605.20512v1, 19 May 2026, with FAccT 2026 formatting; the recorded title and four authors match (PDF p. 1).
Appendices A–E are included on PDF pp. 21–28; participant demographics are in Table 6 on p. 24, and writing-outcome means, SDs and t-tests are in Tables 10–11 on p. 26.

One between-subjects online experiment varies the presence, timing and comparative framing of an AI-values overview. All arms receive GPT-4o autocomplete; No Intervention means no values overview, not no AI (PDF p. 1, abstract; p. 4, section 3 and Table 1; p. 6, section 3.4.2; p. 22, Figure 5).

Condition allocation and preregistration are not stated in the complete document. Explicit random selection concerns writing prompts and sampled essays/suggestions, not allocation to AI-framing groups; assignment.randomized = not_stated, design_class = other, context_class = none and core = unclear are supported. The checker boolean false means a randomized people study is not established by this source (PDF pp. 4–6, Methods; p. 11, section 4.3.1; p. 23, Table 4; p. 27, Appendix E).

The analyzed sample is 149 people with valid responses: No Intervention 40, AI Values 39, Primed + AI Values 34, and comparative 36; 76 are from the United States and 73 from India. These are analyzed counts, not randomized counts, and the total satisfies the minimum sample criterion (PDF p. 5, section 3.2; p. 24, Table 6).
Recruitment required Prolific participants over 18, English fluency, residence in the United States or India, and no more than 6 months abroad (PDF p. 5, section 3.2).

Each participant completed two sequential writing tasks with a 50-word minimum. The first prompt was randomly chosen between food and festival/holiday, and the second between celebrity/public figure and a leave-request email; GPT-4o suggestions were limited to 10 words and retrieved every 500ms (PDF pp. 5–6, sections 3.3–3.4.2; p. 23, Table 4).

Cosine similarity compares different participants' same-topic essays within condition and is an across_people output measure; type-token ratio measures unique words divided by all words within a text and is not between-person diversity (PDF pp. 7–8, section 3.5.2).

Every number in the cosine-similarity reported string matches: AI Values M = 0.462, SD = 0.129; No Intervention M = 0.531, SD = 0.161; t(1575.13) = −10.008, p < .0001, d = −0.477, 95% CI [−∞, −0.057]. The very large degrees of freedom remain inconsistent with the methods' participant-averaging description, as the form already flags (PDF p. 10, section 4.3; p. 26, Tables 10–11; pp. 7–8, section 3.5.2).

Every number in the lexical-diversity reported string matches Tables 10–11: AI Values M = 0.771, SD = 0.071; No Intervention M = 0.782, SD = 0.057; t(147.64) = −1.075, p = 0.086. The unusual p-value is printed in the PDF and is correctly retained as reported (PDF p. 26).

The one-line finding accurately reports 149 analyzed participants, lower cosine similarity in AI Values than No Intervention (0.462 versus 0.531; p < .0001), and no significant increase in lexical diversity; it does not claim confirmed random assignment (PDF p. 5, section 3.2; p. 10, section 4.3; p. 26, Tables 10–11).
This is an original experiment, not a synthesis; no study-count or pooled-estimate entries are warranted (PDF p. 4, Methods; pp. 8–12, Findings).
summary: The recorded counts, quantitative results and source version match the PDF, but the form omits the exclusion rule, similarity-method details and descriptive essay-coded uniqueness outcome. Random assignment to intervention groups is not reported, so a randomized people study cannot be confirmed and core eligibility remains unclear.
